chapter_text:
CHAPTER 21 — BUILDING BLOCKS OF LIFE: CELL AND TISSUES

Introduction

Every living thing — a giant whale, a tall tree, a mushroom or an invisible bacterium — is built from one or more tiny units called CELLS. Just as a brick is the basic unit of a building, the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. Some organisms (bacteria, Amoeba, Paramecium) are made of a single cell and are called unicellular; others, like plants and animals, are made of millions of cells working together and are called multicellular. This chapter explores what cells look like inside, how materials move in and out of them, how they multiply, and how cells of similar kind group together to form tissues, organs and organ systems.

21.1 THE CELL AS THE UNIT OF LIFE

A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all the activities of life — taking in nutrients, releasing energy, growing, responding to stimuli, removing wastes and reproducing. In a unicellular organism a single cell performs all these functions. In a multicellular organism, the work is divided among different kinds of cells. Cells vary greatly in size and shape: a human nerve cell may be over a metre long, a hen's egg is a single large cell, while a typical human cell is only about 10–20 micrometres across. Despite this variety, all cells share the same basic plan.

21.2 DISCOVERY OF THE CELL

In 1665 the English scientist ROBERT HOOKE examined a thin slice of cork (the bark of a tree) under his simple microscope. He saw tiny box-like compartments and named them 'cells' (from the Latin cella, meaning a small room) because they reminded him of the cells in a monastery. What Hooke actually saw were the dead cell walls of cork. Later, Anton van Leeuwenhoek (1674) was the first to observe living cells — bacteria and tiny organisms in pond water — using improved lenses. Robert Brown (1831) discovered the nucleus, and these observations gradually built up our understanding of the cell.

21.3 THE CELL THEORY

In 1838 the botanist MATTHIAS SCHLEIDEN concluded that all plants are made of cells. In 1839 the zoologist THEODOR SCHWANN concluded the same for animals. Together they proposed the CELL THEORY: (1) all living organisms are made of one or more cells, and (2) the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living organisms. In 1855 RUDOLF VIRCHOW added a third idea — 'Omnis cellula e cellula' — that all cells arise from pre-existing cells by division. The modern cell theory therefore states: all organisms are composed of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; and all cells come from previously existing cells.

21.4 PROKARYOTIC AND EUKARYOTIC CELLS

On the basis of nuclear organisation, cells are of two types.
PROKARYOTIC CELLS (pro = primitive, karyon = nucleus) lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus; their genetic material (DNA) lies free in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid. They also lack membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, plastids, endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus. They are small and simple. Examples: bacteria and blue-green algae (cyanobacteria).
EUKARYOTIC CELLS (eu = true) have a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane, and they contain many membrane-bound organelles. They are larger and more complex. Examples: cells of plants, animals, fungi and protists.

21.5 PLANT CELL AND ANIMAL CELL

Both plant and animal cells are eukaryotic and share many organelles, but they differ in a few important ways. A PLANT CELL has a rigid CELL WALL outside its cell membrane, contains PLASTIDS (including green chloroplasts for photosynthesis), and usually has one large central VACUOLE that occupies most of the cell. An ANIMAL CELL has no cell wall (only a cell membrane), has no plastids, has small or no vacuoles, and contains a CENTROSOME (centrioles) that helps in cell division. Because the plant cell has a cell wall and a large vacuole, plant cells tend to have a fixed, often rectangular shape, while animal cells are more rounded and flexible.

21.6 CELL ORGANELLES AND THEIR FUNCTIONS

CELL MEMBRANE (plasma membrane): the thin, living, selectively permeable boundary present in all cells. It separates the cell contents from the surroundings and controls the entry and exit of substances. It is made of lipids and proteins.
CELL WALL: a rigid, non-living, fully permeable outer covering found only in plant cells (and bacteria, fungi). In plants it is made of cellulose. It gives the cell shape, rigidity and protection.
CYTOPLASM: the jelly-like fluid between the cell membrane and the nucleus in which the organelles float. Most chemical reactions of the cell take place here.
NUCLEUS: the dense, rounded 'control centre' of the cell, bounded by a nuclear membrane. It contains the chromosomes (made of DNA), which carry hereditary information and control all cell activities. The dense region inside is the nucleolus.
MITOCHONDRIA: rod-shaped organelles called the 'POWERHOUSE of the cell' because they release energy (ATP) by the breakdown of food during respiration.
ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM (ER): a network of membrane-bound tubes and sheets running through the cytoplasm. ROUGH ER (with ribosomes on its surface) helps make proteins; SMOOTH ER (without ribosomes) helps make fats/lipids. The ER also acts as a channel for transport of materials within the cell.
GOLGI APPARATUS (Golgi body): a stack of flattened membranous sacs that packages, modifies and dispatches materials (such as proteins and secretions) made in the cell. It is sometimes called the 'packaging and dispatch' centre.
RIBOSOMES: very tiny granules, found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the ER, that are the sites of PROTEIN SYNTHESIS.
LYSOSOMES: small sacs filled with powerful digestive enzymes. They digest worn-out parts and foreign material and are nicknamed the 'SUICIDE BAGS of the cell' because they can burst and digest the whole cell when it is damaged.
PLASTIDS: organelles found only in plant cells. CHLOROPLASTS are green plastids containing the pigment chlorophyll; they carry out PHOTOSYNTHESIS (making food using sunlight). Other plastids store pigments (chromoplasts) or food such as starch (leucoplasts).
VACUOLE: a fluid-filled sac bounded by a membrane. Plant cells usually have one LARGE central vacuole that stores water, food and wastes and keeps the cell firm (turgid). Animal cells have small or no vacuoles.

21.7 TRANSPORT ACROSS THE CELL MEMBRANE

The cell membrane is selectively permeable, so it controls what moves in and out. Materials cross it in three main ways.
DIFFUSION is the movement of particles (gases or dissolved substances) from a region of their HIGHER concentration to a region of their LOWER concentration. It needs no energy from the cell. Gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide move in and out of cells by diffusion.
OSMOSIS is a special kind of diffusion: the movement of WATER molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (concentrated solution). When a cell is placed in pure water it gains water and swells (turgid); in a strong salt/sugar solution it loses water and shrinks (plasmolysis in plant cells).
ACTIVE TRANSPORT is the movement of substances ACROSS the membrane AGAINST the concentration gradient (from low to high concentration). Because it goes 'uphill', it requires ENERGY (ATP) supplied by the cell. This is how cells take in some nutrients even when they are already in higher concentration inside.

21.8 CELL DIVISION

New cells arise from existing cells by cell division — this is how organisms grow, repair injuries and reproduce. There are two main types.
MITOSIS occurs in body (somatic) cells. One parent cell divides to form TWO daughter cells, each with the SAME number of chromosomes as the parent. Mitosis is responsible for GROWTH, repair and replacement of cells, and it keeps the chromosome number constant.
MEIOSIS occurs only in the reproductive (germ) cells that form gametes (sperm and eggs / pollen and ovules). One parent cell divides to form FOUR daughter cells, each with HALF the chromosome number of the parent. Meiosis is therefore called reductional division. Its significance is that it keeps the chromosome number constant from generation to generation (when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the full number is restored) and it introduces variation among offspring.

21.9 TISSUES

In a multicellular organism, cells of similar structure that work together to perform a particular function form a TISSUE. The study of tissues is called histology. Grouping cells into tissues allows division of labour, so different jobs are done efficiently.

21.10 PLANT TISSUES

Plant tissues are of two main kinds: meristematic and permanent.
MERISTEMATIC TISSUE consists of small, actively dividing cells with thin walls and dense cytoplasm; it is found at growing points. Apical meristem (at root and shoot tips) increases length; lateral meristem (cambium) increases girth/thickness.
PERMANENT TISSUE is formed when meristematic cells stop dividing and take a permanent shape and function. It is of two types:
  Simple permanent tissues (one cell type): PARENCHYMA — thin-walled living cells that store food and provide support and, when containing chloroplasts (chlorenchyma), perform photosynthesis; COLLENCHYMA — living cells with thickened corners that give flexibility and support to growing parts such as leaf stalks; SCLERENCHYMA — dead cells with very thick, lignified walls that give hardness and strength (for example, the husk of a coconut).
  Complex permanent tissues (more than one cell type; conducting tissues): XYLEM carries WATER and minerals upward from the roots to the leaves and gives mechanical support; PHLOEM carries FOOD (sugars) made in the leaves to all other parts of the plant. Together xylem and phloem form the vascular (conducting) tissue.

21.11 ANIMAL TISSUES

Animal tissues are of four basic types.
EPITHELIAL TISSUE forms the covering or lining of body surfaces, cavities and organs (skin, lining of the mouth, gut and blood vessels). Its cells are tightly packed and it protects underlying parts and helps in absorption and secretion.
CONNECTIVE TISSUE joins, supports and packs together other tissues and organs. Its cells are widely spaced in a matrix. Examples include bone, cartilage, blood (a fluid connective tissue that transports materials), tendons, ligaments and adipose (fat) tissue.
MUSCULAR TISSUE is made of long cells (muscle fibres) that can contract and relax to bring about movement. Striated (skeletal) muscle moves bones and is voluntary; smooth muscle in the walls of internal organs is involuntary; cardiac muscle forms the heart and beats rhythmically throughout life.
NERVOUS TISSUE is made of nerve cells (neurons) that receive and conduct electrical impulses (messages) rapidly from one part of the body to another, coordinating the body's responses. It forms the brain, spinal cord and nerves.

21.12 LEVELS OF ORGANISATION

In a complex organism the body is built up in a series of levels: CELL -> TISSUE -> ORGAN -> ORGAN SYSTEM -> ORGANISM. Similar cells group to form a tissue; different tissues group to form an ORGAN (for example, the stomach is made of epithelial, muscular, connective and nervous tissues working together); several organs that perform a common major function form an ORGAN SYSTEM (for example, the digestive system); and all the organ systems together make up the whole ORGANISM. This organisation allows division of labour and efficient working of the body.

SUMMARY

- The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms. Organisms may be unicellular or multicellular.
- Robert Hooke (1665) first observed and named cells in cork. The cell theory (Schleiden, Schwann; later Virchow) states that all organisms are made of cells, the cell is the unit of life, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
- Prokaryotic cells lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (bacteria); eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus and organelles (plants, animals, fungi).
- Plant cells have a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole; animal cells lack these but have a centrosome.
- Organelles and their roles: cell membrane (controls entry/exit), cell wall (rigidity), nucleus (control centre), mitochondria (powerhouse), ER (transport and synthesis), Golgi body (packaging), ribosomes (protein synthesis), lysosomes (digestion/'suicide bags'), chloroplasts (photosynthesis), vacuole (storage and turgidity).
- Substances cross the membrane by diffusion (high to low, no energy), osmosis (water across a selectively permeable membrane) and active transport (low to high, needs energy).
- Mitosis (in body cells) keeps the chromosome number constant and enables growth and repair; meiosis (in germ cells) halves the chromosome number and forms gametes, ensuring constancy across generations and introducing variation.
- A tissue is a group of similar cells with a common function. Plant tissues: meristematic and permanent (simple: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma; complex: xylem, phloem). Animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.
- Levels of organisation: cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism.

chapter_summary.title: Building Blocks of Life: Cell and Tissues — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 21. It introduces the cell as the basic unit of life, traces the discovery of the cell and the cell theory, compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and plant and animal cells, describes the cell organelles and their functions, explains how materials cross the cell membrane, outlines mitosis and meiosis, and classifies plant and animal tissues and the levels of organisation.

sections.heading: The cell and the cell theory
bullets: The cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all the activities of life; it is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.
Organisms may be unicellular (a single cell, e.g. Amoeba, bacteria) or multicellular (many cells, e.g. plants and animals).
Robert Hooke (1665) first saw and named 'cells' in a slice of cork; van Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells.
The cell theory (Schleiden and Schwann, extended by Virchow) states: all organisms are made of cells, the cell is the unit of life, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

sections.heading: Prokaryotic, eukaryotic, plant and animal cells
bullets: Prokaryotic cells lack a true membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (e.g. bacteria, blue-green algae).
Eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (e.g. plant, animal, fungal cells).
A plant cell has a cell wall, plastids (including chloroplasts) and a large central vacuole.
An animal cell has no cell wall and no plastids, has small or no vacuoles, and possesses a centrosome that helps in cell division.

sections.heading: Cell organelles and their functions
bullets: Cell membrane controls the entry and exit of substances; the nucleus is the control centre containing the chromosomes.
Mitochondria are the powerhouse (release energy); ribosomes carry out protein synthesis; the endoplasmic reticulum transports materials and helps make proteins and fats.
The Golgi apparatus packages and dispatches materials; lysosomes contain digestive enzymes ('suicide bags').
Chloroplasts (green plastids) carry out photosynthesis; the vacuole stores materials and keeps the plant cell turgid.

sections.heading: Transport across the cell membrane and cell division
bullets: Diffusion: movement of particles from higher to lower concentration without using energy (e.g. exchange of O2 and CO2).
Osmosis: movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution.
Active transport: movement of substances against the concentration gradient, requiring energy (ATP).

Mitosis (body cells) gives two daughter cells with the same chromosome number for growth and repair; meiosis (germ cells) gives four cells with half the chromosome number, forming gametes and ensuring constancy across generations.

sections.heading: Tissues and levels of organisation
bullets: A tissue is a group of similar cells performing a common function.
Plant tissues are meristematic (dividing) or permanent; simple permanent tissues are parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma; complex tissues are xylem (carries water) and phloem (carries food).
Animal tissues are of four types: epithelial (covering/lining), connective (support and transport, e.g. blood, bone), muscular (movement) and nervous (conduction of impulses).
Levels of organisation: cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism.

key_takeaways: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life; organisms are unicellular or multicellular.
Robert Hooke discovered and named cells (1665); the cell theory (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow) summarises the central facts about cells.
Prokaryotic cells lack a true nucleus while eukaryotic cells have one; plant cells have a wall, plastids and a large vacuole that animal cells lack.
Key organelles: nucleus (control), mitochondria (energy), chloroplast (photosynthesis), ribosome (protein synthesis), Golgi (packaging), lysosome (digestion), vacuole (storage).
Materials cross the cell membrane by diffusion, osmosis and active transport; only active transport needs energy.
Mitosis keeps the chromosome number constant for growth and repair; meiosis halves it to form gametes.
Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and organ systems form the organism.

A cell without a true membrane-bound nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm (e.g. bacteria).
A cell with a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane and with membrane-bound organelles (e.g. plant and animal cells).
The thin, living, selectively permeable boundary of the cell that controls the entry and exit of substances.
A rigid, non-living, fully permeable outer covering made of cellulose, present only in plant cells; gives shape and support.
The control centre of the cell, bounded by a nuclear membrane, containing the chromosomes (DNA) that carry hereditary information.
Rod-shaped organelles, the 'powerhouse of the cell', that release energy (ATP) during respiration.
A green plastid containing chlorophyll, found in plant cells, that carries out photosynthesis.
A tiny granule, free or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum, that is the site of protein synthesis.
A membrane sac of digestive enzymes that digests worn-out parts and foreign matter; called the 'suicide bag' of the cell.
The movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution.
The movement of substances across the cell membrane against the concentration gradient, requiring energy (ATP).
A group of similar cells that work together to perform a particular function.
A complex plant tissue that conducts water and minerals upward from the roots to the rest of the plant and gives support.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Building Blocks of Life: Cell and Tissues (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-21 for Lesson 21. Attempt all questions. Draw neat labelled diagrams wherever asked.

questions.question: Why is the cell called the basic structural and functional unit of life?
questions.answer: The cell is called the basic STRUCTURAL unit because every living organism is built of one or more cells, just as a building is built of bricks. It is called the basic FUNCTIONAL unit because the cell can independently carry out all the basic activities of life — taking in nutrients, releasing energy by respiration, growth, response to stimuli, removal of wastes and reproduction. In a unicellular organism a single cell performs all these functions; in a multicellular organism the cells together perform them. Below the level of the cell, no smaller unit can carry out all of life's activities. Hence the cell is both the structural and the functional unit of life.
questions.explanation: Structural = building unit; functional = smallest unit that performs all life activities.

questions.question: State the cell theory and name the scientists associated with it.
questions.answer:
The CELL THEORY states: (1) all living organisms are composed of one or more cells; (2) the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living organisms; and (3) all cells arise from pre-existing cells by division.
Scientists: Matthias SCHLEIDEN (1838) showed plants are made of cells; Theodor SCHWANN (1839) showed animals are made of cells — together they proposed the cell theory. Rudolf VIRCHOW (1855) added that all cells come from existing cells ('Omnis cellula e cellula').
questions.explanation: Three statements plus Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow.

questions.question: Give three differences between a plant cell and an animal cell.
questions.answer:
(1) CELL WALL: a plant cell has a rigid cellulose cell wall outside the cell membrane; an animal cell has only a cell membrane (no cell wall).
(2) PLASTIDS: plant cells contain plastids, including green chloroplasts for photosynthesis; animal cells have no plastids.
(3) VACUOLE: a plant cell usually has one large central vacuole; an animal cell has small or no vacuoles.
(Also: animal cells have a centrosome/centrioles which plant cells generally lack.)
questions.explanation: Cell wall, plastids and vacuole are the key differences.

questions.question: Why are mitochondria called the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
questions.answer: Mitochondria are called the 'powerhouse of the cell' because they release the ENERGY needed for all cell activities. During cellular respiration the food (such as glucose) is broken down inside the mitochondria, and the energy released is stored in molecules of ATP (adenosine triphosphate). This ATP is then used to power the cell's work — movement, synthesis of new molecules, active transport and so on. Because the mitochondria are the main sites where energy is released and packaged, they are aptly called the powerhouse.
questions.explanation: They release energy (ATP) by breaking down food during respiration.

questions.question: Differentiate between diffusion and osmosis.
questions.answer:
DIFFUSION is the movement of any particles (gases or dissolved substances) from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration. It does not necessarily involve a membrane and applies to any kind of particle. Example: oxygen and carbon dioxide moving in and out of a cell.
OSMOSIS is a special case of diffusion that applies only to WATER and only across a SELECTIVELY PERMEABLE membrane. Water moves from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (concentrated solution). Example: a raisin swelling when placed in water.
Both are passive (need no energy), but osmosis is specifically the movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane.
questions.explanation: Diffusion = any particles, no membrane needed; osmosis = water only, across a selectively permeable membrane.

questions.question: What is active transport? How does it differ from diffusion?
questions.answer:
ACTIVE TRANSPORT is the movement of a substance across the cell membrane AGAINST its concentration gradient — that is, from a region of LOWER concentration to a region of HIGHER concentration. Because it moves substances 'uphill', it requires ENERGY supplied by the cell in the form of ATP.
It differs from DIFFUSION in two ways: (a) diffusion is movement from higher to lower concentration (down the gradient), whereas active transport is from lower to higher (against the gradient); and (b) diffusion needs NO energy from the cell, whereas active transport DOES need energy. Active transport lets a cell absorb nutrients even when they are already more concentrated inside the cell.
questions.explanation: Active transport: against gradient, needs energy. Diffusion: down gradient, no energy.

questions.question: Compare mitosis and meiosis, and state the significance of each.
questions.answer:
MITOSIS:
 - Occurs in body (somatic) cells.
 - One parent cell divides into TWO daughter cells.
 - Each daughter cell has the SAME number of chromosomes as the parent.
 - Significance: growth of the body, repair and replacement of worn-out or damaged cells; keeps the chromosome number constant in body cells.

MEIOSIS:
 - Occurs only in reproductive (germ) cells that form gametes.
 - One parent cell divides into FOUR daughter cells.
 - Each daughter cell has HALF the chromosome number of the parent (so it is called reductional division).
 - Significance: forms the gametes (sperm/egg, pollen/ovule); because each gamete has half the chromosomes, fusion of two gametes at fertilisation restores the full number — this keeps the chromosome number CONSTANT from one generation to the next. Meiosis also introduces variation among the offspring.

In short: mitosis is for growth and repair (2 identical cells, same chromosome number); meiosis is for sexual reproduction (4 cells, half the chromosome number).
questions.explanation: Mitosis: 2 cells, same number, growth/repair. Meiosis: 4 cells, half number, gametes/variation.

questions.question: Name the four types of animal tissue and state one function of each.
questions.answer:
(1) EPITHELIAL TISSUE — forms the covering and lining of body surfaces and organs (skin, lining of the gut); it protects, and helps in absorption and secretion.
(2) CONNECTIVE TISSUE — joins, supports and packs organs together and transports materials (e.g. bone supports, blood transports).
(3) MUSCULAR TISSUE — its cells contract and relax to bring about movement of the body and its parts.
(4) NERVOUS TISSUE — its cells (neurons) receive and conduct impulses (messages) rapidly, coordinating the body's activities.
questions.explanation: Epithelial (covering), connective (support/transport), muscular (movement), nervous (conduction).

questions.question: Distinguish between simple and complex permanent tissues in plants, giving examples.
questions.answer:
SIMPLE PERMANENT TISSUES are made of ONLY ONE type of cell. The three kinds are: PARENCHYMA (thin-walled living cells that store food and give support), COLLENCHYMA (living cells with thickened corners that give flexibility to growing parts), and SCLERENCHYMA (dead, thick-walled, lignified cells that give hardness and strength).
COMPLEX PERMANENT TISSUES are made of MORE THAN ONE type of cell working together; they are the conducting (vascular) tissues. They are XYLEM (carries water and minerals from roots to leaves and gives support) and PHLOEM (carries food made in the leaves to the rest of the plant).
So simple tissue = one cell type (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma); complex tissue = several cell types forming xylem and phloem.
questions.explanation: Simple = one cell type; complex = several cell types (xylem, phloem).

questions.question: Draw (describe) and explain the levels of organisation in a complex multicellular organism, with an example.
questions.answer:
In a complex organism the body is built up in increasing levels of complexity:
CELL -> TISSUE -> ORGAN -> ORGAN SYSTEM -> ORGANISM.
 - CELL: the basic unit, e.g. a single muscle cell.
 - TISSUE: a group of similar cells doing one job, e.g. muscular tissue formed of many muscle cells.
 - ORGAN: different tissues grouped together to perform a major function, e.g. the STOMACH is made of epithelial, muscular, connective and nervous tissues working together to digest food.
 - ORGAN SYSTEM: several organs that together carry out a major body function, e.g. the DIGESTIVE SYSTEM (mouth, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas) which digests and absorbs food.
 - ORGANISM: all the organ systems together make up the complete living body, e.g. a human being.
This arrangement allows division of labour, so each level does its part and the whole organism functions efficiently.
questions.explanation: Cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism, with the digestive system as an example.

questions.question: Define a cell. Give one example of a unicellular organism.
questions.answer: A CELL is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms — the smallest unit that can carry out all the activities of life. Example of a unicellular organism: Amoeba (or a bacterium / Paramecium).
questions.explanation: Cell = basic unit of life; Amoeba is unicellular.

questions.question: Differentiate between unicellular and multicellular organisms with one example each.
questions.answer: A UNICELLULAR organism is made of only ONE cell, which performs all the life functions; example: Amoeba or bacteria. A MULTICELLULAR organism is made of MANY cells in which work is divided among different cell types; example: a human being or a mango tree.
questions.explanation: One cell vs many cells, with examples.

questions.question: State the three statements of the modern cell theory.
questions.answer: (1) All living organisms are made of one or more cells. (2) The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living organisms. (3) All cells arise from pre-existing cells by division. The first two were given by Schleiden and Schwann; the third was added by Virchow.
questions.explanation: Three points; credit Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow.

questions.question: What did Robert Hooke actually see when he observed cork, and why did he call them cells?
questions.answer: Hooke saw tiny, empty, box-like compartments — actually the dead CELL WALLS of cork. He called them 'cells' because they reminded him of the small rooms (cells) in a monastery; the Latin word 'cella' means a small room.
questions.explanation: Dead cell walls of cork; named after small rooms.

questions.question: Give three differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
questions.answer: (1) NUCLEUS: prokaryotic cells lack a true membrane-bound nucleus (DNA lies free in the nucleoid); eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane. (2) ORGANELLES: prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, plastids, ER, Golgi); eukaryotes possess them. (3) SIZE/COMPLEXITY: prokaryotic cells are small and simple; eukaryotic cells are larger and more complex. Examples: bacteria (prokaryotic); plant/animal cells (eukaryotic).
questions.explanation: Nucleus, organelles, size; with examples.

questions.question: List three structures found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell, and give the function of each.
questions.answer: (1) CELL WALL — a rigid cellulose covering that gives the plant cell shape, rigidity and protection. (2) CHLOROPLASTS (plastids) — green organelles containing chlorophyll that carry out photosynthesis (make food). (3) LARGE CENTRAL VACUOLE — stores water, food and wastes and keeps the cell turgid (firm).
questions.explanation: Cell wall, chloroplast, large vacuole with functions.

questions.question: Name any four cell organelles.
questions.answer: Any four of: nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, ribosomes, lysosomes, plastids (chloroplasts), vacuole, cell membrane.
questions.explanation: Recall of organelle names.

questions.question: What is the function of the cell membrane?
questions.answer: The cell membrane is the thin, living, SELECTIVELY PERMEABLE boundary of the cell. It separates the contents of the cell from the surroundings and CONTROLS the entry and exit of substances into and out of the cell.
questions.explanation: Boundary that controls entry/exit; selectively permeable.

questions.question: State the functions of the nucleus.
questions.answer: The NUCLEUS is the control centre of the cell. It contains the chromosomes (made of DNA), which carry the HEREDITARY information and CONTROL all the activities of the cell, including growth and reproduction.
questions.explanation: Control centre; contains DNA; directs cell activities.

questions.question: Why is the chloroplast important to a plant cell?
questions.answer: The chloroplast contains the green pigment CHLOROPHYLL and is the site of PHOTOSYNTHESIS — the process by which the plant uses sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make its own food (glucose) and release oxygen. Without chloroplasts the plant could not manufacture food.
questions.explanation: Site of photosynthesis; contains chlorophyll.

questions.question: Describe the structure and function of the endoplasmic reticulum.
questions.answer: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a NETWORK of membrane-bound tubes and sheets running through the cytoplasm and connected to the nuclear membrane. It is of two kinds: ROUGH ER, which has ribosomes on its surface and helps make PROTEINS, and SMOOTH ER, which has no ribosomes and helps make FATS (lipids). The ER also serves as a channel for the TRANSPORT of materials within the cell.
questions.explanation: Network of tubes; rough (proteins), smooth (fats); transport.

questions.question: What is the role of the Golgi apparatus?
questions.answer: The Golgi apparatus (Golgi body) is a stack of flattened membranous sacs. It MODIFIES, PACKAGES and DISPATCHES the materials (such as proteins and secretions) made in the cell, sending them to their destinations inside or outside the cell. It is therefore called the packaging and dispatch centre of the cell.
questions.explanation: Packages, modifies and dispatches cell products.

questions.question: Why are lysosomes called 'suicide bags'?
questions.answer: Lysosomes are small sacs containing powerful DIGESTIVE ENZYMES. They digest worn-out cell parts and foreign material. When a cell is damaged or old, the lysosomes may BURST and their enzymes digest the cell's own contents, destroying the cell. Because they can bring about the self-destruction of the cell, they are called 'suicide bags'.
questions.explanation: They can burst and digest the whole (damaged) cell.

questions.question: State two functions of the vacuole in a plant cell.
questions.answer: (1) STORAGE: the large central vacuole stores water, dissolved food, salts and waste products (cell sap). (2) TURGIDITY: by being full of cell sap it keeps the cell firm and turgid, helping the plant keep its shape and stand upright.
questions.explanation: Storage of materials; maintaining turgidity.

questions.question: Define diffusion. Give one example in living cells.
questions.answer: DIFFUSION is the movement of particles of a substance from a region of their HIGHER concentration to a region of their LOWER concentration. It needs no energy. Example: exchange of gases — oxygen diffuses into a cell and carbon dioxide diffuses out.
questions.explanation: High to low concentration; gaseous exchange example.

questions.question: Explain osmosis with the help of an everyday example.
questions.answer: OSMOSIS is the movement of WATER molecules across a SELECTIVELY PERMEABLE membrane from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (concentrated solution). Everyday example: dried raisins or grapes placed in water swell up because water enters them by osmosis. Conversely, if a cell is placed in a strong salt solution, it loses water and shrinks. Osmosis is a special kind of diffusion involving only water and a membrane.
questions.explanation: Water across selectively permeable membrane; raisin example.

questions.question: Compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport in a table-like form.
questions.answer:
DIFFUSION: any particles move from high to low concentration; no membrane required; no energy needed.
OSMOSIS: only WATER moves, from a dilute to a concentrated solution, across a SELECTIVELY PERMEABLE membrane; no energy needed.
ACTIVE TRANSPORT: substances move from LOW to HIGH concentration (against the gradient) across the membrane; ENERGY (ATP) is required.
Thus the first two are passive (no energy), while active transport is the only one that uses energy.
questions.explanation: Direction, what moves, membrane, and energy for each.

questions.question: A cell absorbs a mineral from the soil even though the mineral is already more concentrated inside the cell than outside. Which process is responsible and why?
questions.answer: ACTIVE TRANSPORT is responsible. The mineral is moving from a region of LOWER concentration (outside) to a region of HIGHER concentration (inside) — i.e. against the concentration gradient. Such 'uphill' movement cannot happen by diffusion or osmosis (which only go down the gradient); it needs ENERGY (ATP) supplied by the cell, which is the defining feature of active transport.
questions.explanation: Against the gradient => active transport (uses energy).

questions.question: What is cell division? Name its two main types.
questions.answer: CELL DIVISION is the process by which a parent cell divides to form new daughter cells. It is the way organisms grow, repair injuries and reproduce. Its two main types are MITOSIS (in body cells) and MEIOSIS (in reproductive/germ cells).
questions.explanation: Definition + mitosis and meiosis.

questions.question: State the significance of mitosis.
questions.answer: Mitosis is significant because: (1) it brings about GROWTH of the body by increasing the number of cells; (2) it allows REPAIR and REPLACEMENT of worn-out or damaged cells (e.g. healing of wounds, replacement of skin and blood cells); and (3) it keeps the CHROMOSOME NUMBER CONSTANT, because each daughter cell receives the same number of chromosomes as the parent. In many simple organisms it is also a means of asexual reproduction.
questions.explanation: Growth, repair/replacement, constant chromosome number.

questions.question: State the significance of meiosis.
questions.answer: Meiosis is significant because: (1) it produces the GAMETES (sperm/egg, pollen/ovule) needed for sexual reproduction; (2) it HALVES the chromosome number in the gametes, so that when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the normal (full) chromosome number is restored — this keeps the chromosome number CONSTANT from generation to generation; and (3) it introduces VARIATION among the offspring, which is important for evolution.
questions.explanation: Forms gametes; halves chromosomes; maintains number; variation.

questions.question: Give three differences between mitosis and meiosis.
questions.answer: (1) SITE: mitosis occurs in body (somatic) cells; meiosis occurs in reproductive (germ) cells. (2) NUMBER OF DAUGHTER CELLS: mitosis gives 2 daughter cells; meiosis gives 4. (3) CHROMOSOME NUMBER: in mitosis the daughter cells have the SAME number as the parent; in meiosis they have HALF the number. (Mitosis is for growth/repair; meiosis is for gamete formation.)
questions.explanation: Site, number of cells, chromosome number.

questions.question: Define a tissue. Give one example each of a plant and an animal tissue.
questions.answer: A TISSUE is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a particular function. Example of a plant tissue: xylem (or parenchyma). Example of an animal tissue: muscular tissue (or blood/epithelial tissue).
questions.explanation: Definition + one plant and one animal example.

questions.question: What is meristematic tissue? Where is it found?
questions.answer: MERISTEMATIC TISSUE is plant tissue made of small, actively DIVIDING cells with thin walls and dense cytoplasm. It is found at the GROWING POINTS of the plant — at the tips of roots and shoots (apical meristem) and in the cambium (lateral meristem) which increases the girth of stems and roots.
questions.explanation: Dividing tissue at growing points (root/shoot tips, cambium).

questions.question: Name the three simple permanent tissues in plants and give one feature of each.
questions.answer: (1) PARENCHYMA — thin-walled living cells that store food and provide support (and perform photosynthesis when they contain chloroplasts). (2) COLLENCHYMA — living cells with thickened corners that give flexibility and support to growing parts such as leaf stalks. (3) SCLERENCHYMA — dead cells with very thick, lignified walls that give hardness and strength (e.g. coconut husk).
questions.explanation: Parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma with a feature each.

questions.question: Compare the functions of xylem and phloem.
questions.answer: XYLEM is a complex tissue that conducts WATER and dissolved minerals UPWARD from the roots to the stem and leaves, and also provides mechanical support. PHLOEM is a complex tissue that conducts FOOD (sugars made in the leaves by photosynthesis) to all other parts of the plant. Together they form the vascular (conducting) tissue.
questions.explanation: Xylem = water (upward); phloem = food (to all parts).

questions.question: Name the four types of animal tissue and give one example of each.
questions.answer: (1) EPITHELIAL TISSUE — e.g. the lining of the mouth or the outer layer of skin. (2) CONNECTIVE TISSUE — e.g. blood, bone, cartilage, tendons. (3) MUSCULAR TISSUE — e.g. the muscles attached to bones, or cardiac muscle of the heart. (4) NERVOUS TISSUE — e.g. the brain, spinal cord and nerves (neurons).
questions.explanation: Four tissue types each with an example.

questions.question: Why is blood considered a connective tissue?
questions.answer: Blood is considered a CONNECTIVE tissue because its cells (red cells, white cells and platelets) are widely separated and float in a fluid MATRIX called plasma — the typical plan of connective tissue, whose cells lie in a matrix. Blood connects different parts of the body by TRANSPORTING oxygen, food, wastes, hormones and heat between them.
questions.explanation: Cells in a fluid matrix (plasma); it connects/transports.

questions.question: Explain the levels of organisation in a multicellular organism with an example.
questions.answer: The body of a complex organism is organised in levels: CELL -> TISSUE -> ORGAN -> ORGAN SYSTEM -> ORGANISM. Similar cells form a TISSUE (e.g. muscle cells form muscular tissue); different tissues form an ORGAN (e.g. the stomach, made of epithelial, muscular, connective and nervous tissues); several organs form an ORGAN SYSTEM (e.g. the digestive system); and all the organ systems together make the complete ORGANISM (e.g. a human). This allows division of labour for efficient working.
questions.explanation: Cell->tissue->organ->organ system->organism, with example.

questions.question: A coconut husk is hard and fibrous, while the soft pulp of a fruit is easily squashed. Relate this difference to plant tissues.
questions.answer: The HARDNESS of a coconut husk is due to SCLERENCHYMA — dead cells with very thick, lignified walls that provide great strength and rigidity. The SOFTNESS of fruit pulp is due to PARENCHYMA — thin-walled living cells that mainly store food and water and give little mechanical strength. Thus the type of permanent tissue present (thick-walled sclerenchyma vs thin-walled parenchyma) explains the difference in texture and hardness.
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma (hard husk) vs parenchyma (soft pulp).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In 1665 Robert Hooke cut a thin slice of cork and examined it under his microscope. He saw rows of tiny box-like compartments and gave them a name. Much later, Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow built up the cell theory.

(i) What did Hooke call the box-like compartments and why?
(ii) What were the structures he actually saw?
(iii) State two statements of the cell theory.
(iv) What did Virchow add to the cell theory?
questions.answer:
(i) He called them 'CELLS' because they looked like the small rooms (cells) of a monastery; 'cella' means a small room in Latin.
(ii) He actually saw the dead CELL WALLS of cork cells (the living contents had gone).
(iii) Any two of: all organisms are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
(iv) Virchow added that all cells arise from PRE-EXISTING cells by division ('Omnis cellula e cellula').
questions.explanation: Tests recall of Hooke's observation and the cell theory.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student looks at two cells under a microscope. Cell A has a rigid outer wall, green bodies inside, and one large vacuole filling most of the cell. Cell B has no wall, no green bodies, only small vacuoles, and a small structure that helps in division.

(i) Which cell is a plant cell and which is an animal cell?
(ii) Name the rigid outer wall and the green bodies in cell A.
(iii) Name the structure in cell B that helps in division.
(iv) Give one feature common to both cells.
questions.answer:
(i) Cell A is a PLANT cell; cell B is an ANIMAL cell.
(ii) The rigid outer wall is the CELL WALL (made of cellulose); the green bodies are CHLOROPLASTS.
(iii) The structure that helps in division in cell B is the CENTROSOME (centrioles).
(iv) Common feature (any one): both have a cell membrane, a true nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria and ribosomes (both are eukaryotic).
questions.explanation: Applies plant vs animal cell differences to identify cells.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The cell is like a busy factory. The nucleus directs the work, mitochondria supply the power, ribosomes make the products, the Golgi body packs them, and lysosomes clean up the waste.

(i) Which organelle is the 'control centre'?
(ii) Which organelle is the 'powerhouse', and what does it produce?
(iii) Which organelle synthesises proteins?
(iv) Which organelle packs and dispatches the products?
questions.answer:
(i) The NUCLEUS is the control centre (it contains the chromosomes/DNA).
(ii) The MITOCHONDRION is the powerhouse; it releases energy stored as ATP during respiration.
(iii) The RIBOSOMES synthesise proteins.
(iv) The GOLGI APPARATUS (Golgi body) packs and dispatches the products.
questions.explanation: Matches organelles to their functions using the factory analogy.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Gland cells that secrete large amounts of protein and enzymes are packed with ribosomes, rough endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi bodies and many mitochondria.

(i) Why does such a cell need many ribosomes and rough ER?
(ii) Why does it need many Golgi bodies?
(iii) Why does it need many mitochondria?
(iv) Name the organelle that would dispose of worn-out parts in this cell.
questions.answer:
(i) Ribosomes and rough ER are the sites of PROTEIN SYNTHESIS — a cell making lots of protein needs many of them.
(ii) Golgi bodies MODIFY, PACK and DISPATCH the proteins/secretions, so a secretory cell needs many of them.
(iii) Making and exporting so much protein needs a lot of ENERGY (ATP), supplied by the mitochondria.
(iv) LYSOSOMES dispose of worn-out parts and waste ('suicide bags').
questions.explanation: Relates organelle abundance to cell function.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A few raisins are placed in a beaker of plain water. After some hours they become swollen. The same raisins, if then placed in strong sugar syrup, shrink again.

(i) Name the process responsible for the swelling.
(ii) In which direction does water move when the raisins swell?
(iii) Why do the raisins shrink in sugar syrup?
(iv) Does this process need energy from the cell?
questions.answer:
(i) The process is OSMOSIS.
(ii) Water moves INTO the raisins — from the surrounding water (higher water concentration) into the raisin (lower water concentration), across the selectively permeable membrane.
(iii) In sugar syrup the water concentration outside is lower than inside, so water moves OUT of the raisins by osmosis and they shrink.
(iv) No — osmosis is a passive process and needs no energy from the cell.
questions.explanation: Applies osmosis to the raisin experiment.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Three statements describe movement across the cell membrane: (P) oxygen entering a cell; (Q) water entering a root hair from the soil; (R) a mineral ion being pumped into a cell against its concentration gradient.

(i) Name the process in P.
(ii) Name the process in Q.
(iii) Name the process in R.
(iv) Which of P, Q, R needs energy?
questions.answer:
(i) P is DIFFUSION (a gas moving from high to low concentration).
(ii) Q is OSMOSIS (water moving across a selectively permeable membrane).
(iii) R is ACTIVE TRANSPORT (movement against the concentration gradient).
(iv) Only R (active transport) needs energy (ATP); diffusion and osmosis are passive.
questions.explanation: Distinguishes the three transport processes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A body cell with 46 chromosomes undergoes mitosis. A germ cell with 46 chromosomes undergoes meiosis to form gametes.

(i) How many cells are formed by mitosis, and how many chromosomes does each have?
(ii) How many cells are formed by meiosis, and how many chromosomes does each have?
(iii) Why is meiosis called reductional division?
(iv) How is the chromosome number restored in the offspring?
questions.answer:
(i) Mitosis forms 2 daughter cells, each with 46 chromosomes (same as the parent).
(ii) Meiosis forms 4 daughter cells, each with 23 chromosomes (half the parent number).
(iii) Because it REDUCES the chromosome number to half (from 46 to 23) in the gametes.
(iv) At fertilisation, a male gamete (23) fuses with a female gamete (23) to give a zygote with 46 chromosomes — the full number is restored.
questions.explanation: Applies chromosome numbers to mitosis and meiosis.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

When you cut your finger, the wound heals over a few days as new skin cells are formed. The formation of egg and sperm cells, however, involves a different kind of division.

(i) Which type of cell division heals the wound?
(ii) Which type of division forms eggs and sperm?
(iii) State one significance of the division in (i).
(iv) State one significance of the division in (ii).
questions.answer:
(i) MITOSIS heals the wound (it forms new identical body cells).
(ii) MEIOSIS forms eggs and sperm (gametes).
(iii) Significance of mitosis: growth and repair/replacement of cells, keeping the chromosome number constant.
(iv) Significance of meiosis: it forms gametes with half the chromosome number, keeping the species' chromosome number constant across generations and introducing variation.
questions.explanation: Connects mitosis to repair and meiosis to gamete formation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A cross-section of a plant stem shows several tissues: a layer of dividing cells, thin-walled storage cells, thick-walled dead supporting cells, and tubes that carry water and food.

(i) Name the layer of dividing cells.
(ii) Name the thin-walled storage cells.
(iii) Name the thick-walled dead supporting cells.
(iv) Name the two tissues that carry water and food.
questions.answer:
(i) The dividing cells are MERISTEMATIC tissue (e.g. cambium).
(ii) The thin-walled storage cells are PARENCHYMA.
(iii) The thick-walled dead supporting cells are SCLERENCHYMA.
(iv) Water is carried by XYLEM and food by PHLOEM (the vascular/conducting tissues).
questions.explanation: Identifies plant tissues from their descriptions.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The human stomach is made of an inner lining, layers of muscle, a supporting layer with blood vessels, and nerves. Together they digest and churn food.

(i) Name the tissue that forms the inner lining.
(ii) Name the tissue that churns the food.
(iii) Name the tissue type to which blood belongs.
(iv) Since several tissues work together, what level of organisation is the stomach?
questions.answer:
(i) The inner lining is EPITHELIAL tissue.
(ii) The churning is done by MUSCULAR tissue.
(iii) Blood is a CONNECTIVE tissue.
(iv) Because several different tissues work together, the stomach is an ORGAN (the level above tissue: cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism).
questions.explanation: Connects the four tissue types to an organ and levels of organisation.
